summary.headline: A good renewable power business, but the price already counts on projects still being built
summary.text: Vidullanka PLC (VLL.N0000 voting, VLL.X0000 non-voting) runs 76 MW of hydro, solar and biomass plants, and most of its profit comes from two dollar-tariff hydro plants in Uganda. It passes all four business tests: ROE of 15–19% for five years, net debt 0.68x equity, a profit of over Rs 1bn for four years running, and a dividend paid every year. Results are softening, though. Owners' profit for the half to September 2026 rose 13% to Rs 671mn only because of Rs 245mn of unexplained other income. The September quarter fell 58% as finance costs doubled on borrowing for battery storage and new solar plants, and net debt doubled to Rs 6.85bn in six months. At Rs 22.10 (voting, 30 September; check the live price) the share is 2.26x NAV of Rs 9.76 and about 15x trailing EPS. Five methods put fair value at about Rs 8.95. I'd buy at up to Rs 7.60 and treat Rs 6.70 or less as a strong buy. The market is paying now for projects that haven't yet earned anything.

fullText:
VIDULLANKA PLC (VLL.N0000 voting, VLL.X0000 non-voting): long-term valuation, 2026-11-17

SUMMARY
Vidullanka is a renewable power producer with 76 MW of hydro, solar and biomass ("dendro") plants in Sri Lanka and two hydro plants in Uganda, which earn most of its profit. It is a good business on all four tests: return on equity of 15–19% for five years, net debt 0.68x equity, a profit of more than Rs 1bn for four years running, and cash flow that pays a dividend each year. But at Rs 22.10 (voting, last trade 30 September 2026; check the live price) the share is 2.26x book value and about 15x trailing earnings. On five methods fair value is about Rs 8.95. I'd buy at up to Rs 7.60 and treat Rs 6.70 or less as a strong buy. The price assumes that the battery storage, wind and new solar projects will earn far more than the cost of capital. That may happen, but it isn't in the figures yet. Watch list (category 2).

THE BUSINESS
- Overseas hydro (Muvumbe and Bukinda, 6.5 MW each, Uganda): revenue Rs 2.55bn and profit Rs 1.21bn in 2025/26, about three-quarters of group profit. The tariff is set in US dollars (Bukinda Rs 31.13, USD 0.0957 a unit, with 15 years of contract left). Profits sent home pay 15–20% withholding tax.
- Local mini-hydro (12 plants including joint ventures): revenue Rs 0.53bn and profit Rs 0.42bn. Several contracts have been renewed (Batathota to 2041, Gurugoda to 2044, Bambarabatuoya to 2036); Lower Kotmale has 8 years left.
- Solar: 21 MW added in 2025/26 through four projects, plus the Vavunathivu 10 MW plants held through Solar Universe, a joint venture with WindForce. The 10 MW Ranna plant was due on the grid in September 2026.
- Dendro and plantation: Dehiattakandiya 3.3 MW (51% joint venture). Medawachchiya 6.6 MW is under construction (Rs 1.3bn equity commitment, Rs 0.5bn put in, commissioning mid-2027/28).
- New lines: a 49% stake in Storex, building twelve 10 MW / 40 MWh battery storage sites (Rs 2.2bn invested in the half-year); a 30% stake in the 10 MW Alankuda wind plant; the 50 MW Mullikulam wind tender (with the David Peiris group); and lowest bidder, with Skipper, for a Rs 5bn transmission line for the CEB.
- Buyers: the CEB and its new National System Operator in Sri Lanka, and UETCL in Uganda. The report mentions payment delays during the CEB's restructuring, and output curtailed by the grid: Rs 119mn of lost energy from March 2025 to September 2026.

LATEST RESULTS
Six months to 30 September 2026 (unaudited): revenue Rs 2.04bn (+6%), gross profit Rs 1.43bn (+2%), profit to owners Rs 671mn (+13%). The rise came from Rs 300mn of other income, Rs 245mn of which the cash flow statement removes as non-cash and the report doesn't explain. Finance costs more than doubled to Rs 357mn. The September quarter alone was weak: profit to owners Rs 131mn against Rs 311mn (−58%), with finance costs Rs 210mn (+161%) and cost of sales up 28%. EPS for the half is about Rs 0.65 on all 1,038mn shares; the report shows Rs 0.70 because it divides by 954mn shares (voting only, it seems), unlike the annual report, which counts both classes.
Balance sheet: net debt (borrowings and leases less cash) rose from Rs 3.35bn in March to Rs 6.85bn in September, as Rs 1.96bn went on plant and Rs 1.89bn into new projects (mainly Storex). NAV per share Rs 9.76. Interim dividend Rs 0.20 (Rs 0.35 a year earlier).
Year to March 2026 (audited): revenue Rs 3.83bn (Rs 5.42bn a year earlier, which included Rs 2.1bn from a finished engineering contract in Guyana). Profit after tax Rs 1.55bn (Rs 1.58bn), owners Rs 1.49bn, EPS Rs 1.45 (Rs 1.56). Generation 229 GWh (+15%), capacity 76 MW (51 MW). Dividends Rs 0.65 (Rs 1.70, of which Rs 1.20 was paid in shares).

REINVESTMENT AND GROWTH
2025/26 was a heavy build year: capex booked Rs 2.73bn (including Rs 1.64bn of solar plant for the four new projects and Rs 0.68bn of land) against depreciation of Rs 0.44bn, plus Rs 0.66bn into joint ventures and projects. That spending is mostly growth, judged on its return, not upkeep. Net debt rose by more than half the capex, so it was largely borrowed. The calculator gives a reinvestment rate of 198% of after-tax operating profit at a 16.6% return on capital: supported growth of 32.8%. That figure is inflated by one build year. I assume 3% / 6% / 9% for five years, well inside it, because each new project also needs new money. Long-run growth is 3 / 4 / 5%, below the 12.24% bond yield and WACC, with reinvestment of growth ÷ return on capital.
Maintenance capex: the company gives no split. The calculator's range is Rs 1.43bn / 0.77bn / 0.44bn, but its top two figures are distorted by the build year. For plants on long contracts, depreciation (about Rs 0.55bn a year now) is a fair base. Bear Rs 0.75bn, base Rs 0.55bn, bull Rs 0.44bn.
Cash: FY2026 cash from operations was Rs 1.34bn after Rs 0.93bn of tax paid (including tax on Ugandan dividends), against dividends of Rs 0.75bn including minorities. On that year's cash after maintenance capex (Rs 0.57bn by the calculator) the dividend wasn't covered. On a more normal year (after-tax operating profit of about Rs 1.5bn plus depreciation, less upkeep and after-tax interest) it is covered about 1.5 times. The lower interim suggests the board is holding cash back for the projects.

REQUIRED RETURN
Cost of equity = risk-free 8.24% (12.24% 10-year bond less a 4.0% default spread) + beta 0.70 × (4.2% mature premium + 6.08% country premium) = 15.4%; bear 16.9%, bull 13.9%. The beta (provisional) is Damodaran's global Green & Renewable Energy unlevered beta of 0.57 (a web-search figure, January 2026; his emerging-markets file couldn't be opened), relevered at net debt of 0.30x market value. Only one local 5-year beta was found (0.28), so step 4 is incomplete. This is inside the 12–22% range for CSE shares, at the lower end because contracted power is steady. No extra premium is added for Uganda, although most of the profit comes from there. Cost of debt 9.56% (interest paid ÷ average borrowings and leases, FY2026), after tax 7.2%. WACC 13.5% (debt weight 23%); bear 14.7%, bull 12.3%.

VALUATION
Methods: a whole-company DCF of the consolidated plants (at WACC, less net debt) plus the joint ventures and project stakes; P/E; justified price to book; residual income; and a two-stage dividend model. Fair value weights each scenario's average 30/50/20.
- Whole-company DCF (WACC, less net debt) + joint ventures and projects: Rs 3.44 / 9.26 / 19.05 (weighted 9.47). Consolidated plants valued as a whole company: cash before interest after maintenance capex Rs 1.10 / 1.48 / 1.80bn (after-tax operating profit Rs 1.30 / 1.48 / 1.69bn, excluding joint ventures, plus depreciation of about Rs 0.55bn, less maintenance Rs 0.75 / 0.55 / 0.44bn), growing 3% / 6% / 9% for five years then 3% / 4% / 5%, less the reinvestment that growth needs at a 12% / 15% / 17% return on capital, at WACC 14.7% / 13.5% / 12.3%, less net debt Rs 6.85bn at 30 September 2026. Firm value Rs 6.8 / 12.1 / 20.3bn gives Rs −0.03 / 5.04 / 12.95 a share (bear taken as nil). Value after year 5: 58% / 70% / 80%; the bull is over the 75% flag, so most of it rests on the long run. Plus joint ventures (Rs 2.43bn book) and project investments, mainly the Storex battery storage stake (Rs 2.21bn at cost), less minorities (Rs 0.26bn): 85% and 80% of book in the bear, book in the base, joint ventures at 1.35x and projects at 1.5x cost in the bull: Rs 3.44 / 4.22 / 6.10 a share.
- P/E method: Rs 6.62 / 9.37 / 13.02 (weighted 9.28). EPS for the year to March 2027 of Rs 1.15 / 1.35 / 1.50 times 5.8 / 6.9 / 8.7, the forward P/E justified at the cost of equity when growth is paid for (payout = 1 − growth ÷ ROE; ROE 14 / 16 / 17%, growth 4 / 5 / 6%). Base EPS is 11% below the Rs 1.51 last-12-months figure because that includes Rs 0.245bn of unexplained other income (about Rs 0.24 a share) and finance costs have doubled on new borrowing for projects not yet earning; without the item the run-rate is about Rs 1.28.
- Justified price to book: Rs 7.57 / 10.32 / 13.59 (weighted 10.15). (ROE − growth) ÷ (cost of equity − growth) × NAV Rs 9.76: ROE 14 / 16 / 17%, growth 4 / 5 / 6%, cost of equity 16.9 / 15.4 / 13.9%, giving 0.78 / 1.06 / 1.39x book. Rs 22.10 is 2.26x book, which would need a lasting ROE of about 28% at the base cost of equity.
- Residual income: Rs 7.07 / 10.47 / 14.53 (weighted 10.26). Book value Rs 9.76 (September 2026); ROE 14 / 16 / 17% for ten years with 45% paid out, cost of equity 16.9 / 15.4 / 13.9%, then the excess return grows at 4 / 5 / 6%. ROE sits close to the cost of equity, so little is added to book.
- Dividends (two-stage): Rs 3.60 / 5.59 / 8.90 (weighted 5.66). Dividend for 2026/27 of Rs 0.50 / 0.60 / 0.70 (Rs 0.20 interim so far against Rs 0.35 a year earlier; Rs 0.65 for 2025/26), growing 3 / 6 / 9% for five years then 3 / 4 / 5%, at the cost of equity 16.9 / 15.4 / 13.9%. Growth is within the supported rate. Lowest of the methods because the company keeps more than half its profit for new plants.
Averages: bear Rs 5.66, base Rs 9.00, bull Rs 13.82. Fair value Rs 8.95 (0.92x NAV). Buy price Rs 7.60 (15% below), strong buy Rs 6.70 (25% below).
Ratio checks: beta 0.70, cost of equity 15.4% and WACC 13.5% (below the cost of equity) are in range. Net debt/EBITDA is about 2.5x (trailing EBITDA about Rs 2.7bn, including the unexplained Rs 0.245bn), under 3x. Vidullanka also guarantees Rs 1.64bn of joint-venture loans. The chosen P/Es (5.8–8.7x) and P/Bs (0.78–1.39x) are the justified figures, so they imply no more growth than is supported.

WHY THE MARKET PAYS MORE
At Rs 22.10 the market values the company at about Rs 22.8bn plus Rs 6.85bn of net debt, against trailing EBITDA of about Rs 2.7bn: about 9.4x after taking out the Rs 4.6bn of joint-venture and project stakes. Buyers are paying for the pipeline: battery storage at 12 sites, wind, more solar and the transmission line. If those earn well above the 13–15% cost of capital, the bull case rises. But most of them are still being built or bid for, the first effect has been higher debt and finance costs, and the existing solar contracts were cut in tariff by the off-taker. I value the new projects at cost (1.5x in the bull case) until they produce results.

BUY PLAN (500 shares)
200 shares up to Rs 7.60, 150 up to Rs 7.15, 150 up to Rs 6.70: average about Rs 7.20, total about Rs 3,600 (Rs 11,050 at Rs 22.10).
Realism: Rs 7.60 needs a fall of about 66%. The voting share traded at Rs 19.90–23.40 in the September quarter, and the lowest figure I could find for the past year is about Rs 12.40 (Simply Wall St, December 2025 snapshot). It isn't likely soon. The non-voting share (Rs 20.30 at 30 September) is a little cheaper and has the same rights to profit.

WHAT WOULD CHANGE THE VIEW
Higher: battery storage sites commissioned and earning (Storex), with tariffs known; Medawachchiya and the wind projects running to budget; the CEB/NSO paying on time and curtailment ending; Uganda contracts extended.
Lower: further profit drops like the September quarter; debt rising faster than new plants come on line; the CEB cutting tariffs or curtailing more; poor rainfall in Uganda or Sri Lanka; the rupee strengthening against the dollar (lowering Ugandan profit in rupees); trouble at joint ventures whose loans Vidullanka guarantees.

UNCERTAINTIES
- The Rs 245mn of 'other income' in the half-year isn't explained in the interim report.
- The interim EPS uses 954mn shares, not the 1,038mn in issue; I've recomputed it.
- Muvumbe's remaining contract term isn't given in the reports read (Bukinda's is 15 years).
- Prices are from the interim report (30 September 2026); the CSE couldn't be reached from this run. The site shows the latest CSE close once fetched.
- Beta inputs come from web-search extracts and are provisional.
- FY2022–FY2024 figures come from the ten-year summary only (no reinvestment figures for those years).
